claims.text: Structural and chemical stability of equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles from 473–1923 K is governed by the interplay between local lattice distortion and chemical short-range order.
Differences in constituent atomic sizes induce local lattice distortion.
Strong lattice distortion combined with minimal pre-existing SRO creates a rugged energy landscape.
The rugged energy landscape produces uniformly high activation barriers for atomic diffusion throughout a nanoparticle.
High diffusion barriers retard self-diffusion.
Retarded atomic diffusion suppresses phase separation.
Retarded atomic diffusion suppresses grain growth.
Retarded atomic diffusion suppresses elemental segregation.
Minimal SRO prevents nucleation of energetically favorable elemental clusters.
The combination of strong lattice distortion and minimal SRO limits formation of antiphase boundaries and secondary phases.
Significant SRO creates local differences in atomic mobility.
Local differences in atomic mobility drive phase separation at high temperature.
Pronounced SRO promotes elemental clustering and the emergence of secondary phases during heating.
An equiatomic five-component solid solution can exist with minimal initial SRO.
Nanoparticles with strong lattice distortion and suppressed initial SRO will retain a single-phase structure after high-temperature treatment.
Nanoparticles with strong lattice distortion and suppressed initial SRO will exhibit minimal grain growth after high-temperature treatment.
Nanoparticles with strong lattice distortion and suppressed initial SRO will retain a homogeneous elemental distribution after high-temperature treatment.
Samples with higher initial SRO or lower lattice distortion will show increasingly severe phase separation as temperature rises.
Substrate-induced surface diffusion or uncontrolled environmental factors can override intrinsic stability effects associated with lattice distortion and SRO.
Rapid quenching minimizes SRO, whereas mild pre-annealing permits partial SRO formation.
